report.source_text: Imaging studies included a normal chest X-ray, along with abdominal and pelvic ultrasound findings that were also unremarkable. A head and neck computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a multilobulated hyperdense ulcerative scalp lesion located on the right frontal region of the scalp, measuring 9 × 7.8 × 6 cm. Notably, there was no skull bone erosion, and no intracranial extension of the mass was observed. Enlarged bilateral cervical lymph nodes were seen at levels I and II. Additionally, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine showed a pathological compression fracture of the T10 vertebral body with no stenosis of the canal, raising a high suspicion for vertebral metastasis (Fig. 2).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 49-year-old female of African origin presented with a recurrent scalp mass following incomplete excision 5 months prior without histopathological analysis. The mass had been present for over 10 years, initially non-progressive, but recurred with ulceration and bleeding tendency. Physical examination revealed two right-sided scalp lesions: a 9×7 cm fungating, tender, bleeding mass and a 3×3 cm non-fungating lesion. CT imaging demonstrated a 9×7.8×6 cm multilobulated hyperdense ulcerative lesion without skull bone erosion or intracranial extension. Staging evaluation revealed enlarged bilateral cervical lymph nodes (levels I and II) and a T10 vertebral pathological compression fracture suspicious for metastasis, but normal chest X-ray and abdominal/pelvic ultrasound. Baseline laboratory studies were normal. Biopsy confirmed mucoepidermoid carcinoma. The patient underwent definitive surgical excision and at 8-month follow-up showed no clinical signs of recurrence, with stable vertebral fracture managed conservatively.
